after.worked_solution:
Since $x=5$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-5)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-5)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-5)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-5)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $5$ | $1$ | $-8$ | $5$ | $-50$ |
|  | $↓$ | $5$ | $-15$ | $-50$ |
|  | $1$ | $-3$ | $-10$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x-5}={x}^{2}-3x-10,
$$

which means that

$$
p(x)=(x-5)({x}^{2}-3x-10).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x-5)(x+2)(x-5) \\  & =(x+2)(x-5)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x-5)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=5$ has multiplicity $2.$

a

b
 (x5+y2)(x−y4)

d

$$
{a}^{2}-{b}^{2}=(a+b)(a-b)
$$

Notice that our expression can be written as a difference of squares:

$$
{x}^{4}-{y}^{6}={({x}^{2})}^{2}-{({y}^{3})}^{2}
$$

Finally, we factor our expression using the difference of squares formula:

$$
{({x}^{2})}^{2}-{({y}^{3})}^{2}=({x}^{2}+{y}^{3})({x}^{2}-{y}^{3})
$$

$$
